subtopic_detail: Penicillin regimen for syphilis seroconversion detected on third trimester screening
stem:
You are the registrar in a regional antenatal clinic. A 30-year-old woman at 28 weeks in her first pregnancy is recalled after her routine third trimester screening bloods.

Her booking serology at 10 weeks was negative for syphilis. The current sample is reactive on treponemal enzyme immunoassay, reactive on Treponema pallidum particle agglutination, and shows a rapid plasma reagin titre of 1:32.

She feels well and has no rash, no genital ulceration and no lymphadenopathy. She has had one new sexual partner in the past 5 months. She has never been treated for syphilis and has no allergies to any medication, including penicillin. Her human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology are negative and a detailed ultrasound today shows a structurally normal foetus with normal growth and liquor volume.

data_table.Examination: No rash, no genital ulceration, no lymphadenopathy, symphysis-fundal height appropriate for dates
data_table.Investigations: Treponemal enzyme immunoassay reactive, Treponema pallidum particle agglutination reactive, rapid plasma reagin 1:32; booking syphilis serology at 10 weeks negative; human immunodeficiency virus and hepatitis serology negative
data_table.Imaging: Ultrasound today shows normal foetal anatomy, growth and liquor volume

lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose, with a repeat rapid plasma reagin titre in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Macrolide resistance in Treponema pallidum is widespread and azithromycin does not reliably cross the placenta, so it cannot be relied on to treat the foetus. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly, with a second identical dose one week later
options.rationale: A negative result at 10 weeks with a titre of 1:32 now establishes infection acquired within the past 18 weeks, which is early syphilis, and Australian guidance adds a second dose one week after the first when the woman is pregnant to reduce the risk of treatment failure and congenital infection. Penicillin is the only agent that reliably treats the foetus as well as the mother. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines
RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly as a single dose, with no further injections
options.rationale: A single dose is the standard regimen for early syphilis outside pregnancy, but a second dose is added in pregnancy because of the higher stakes of treatment failure for the foetus. This is the near-pair to know by pregnancy status rather than by stage. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Benzathine benzylpenicillin 1.8 g intramuscularly weekly for three doses over three weeks
options.rationale: Three weekly doses is the regimen for late latent syphilis or infection of unknown duration; a documented negative test 18 weeks earlier dates this infection as early and makes the longer course unnecessary. (Source: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines

options.text: Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 14 days, with a repeat rapid plasma reagin at delivery
options.rationale: Doxycycline is the non-pregnant alternative for penicillin-allergic patients; it is contraindicated in the second and third trimesters because of effects on foetal teeth and bone, and it does not treat the foetus. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Australia has seen a sustained resurgence of infectious syphilis, with congenital cases returning in several jurisdictions, which is why repeat third trimester screening has been reinstated in many antenatal programmes alongside booking and delivery testing. Staging determines the regimen: early syphilis, meaning primary, secondary or early latent infection acquired within the past 2 years, is treated with benzathine penicillin, while late latent disease or infection of unknown duration requires three weekly doses. A documented negative test within the previous 2 years is what allows infection to be staged as early. Penicillin is the only agent that reliably crosses the placenta at treponemicidal concentrations, so a woman with genuine penicillin allergy must be desensitised rather than given an alternative. Response is monitored by a fourfold fall in the rapid plasma reagin titre, and the neonate requires assessment and follow-up regardless of maternal response.
key_points: A negative test within the past 2 years stages the infection as early and shortens the regimen
Pregnant women with early syphilis receive a second benzathine penicillin dose one week after the first
Penicillin is the only agent that reliably treats the foetus; allergic women are desensitised rather than substituted
Three weekly doses are reserved for late latent syphilis or infection of unknown duration
Monitor treatment response with a fourfold fall in rapid plasma reagin titre and notify the case
explanation.pearls: Warn about the Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction within 24 hours of the first dose: in the third trimester it can provoke uterine contractions and transient foetal heart rate abnormalities, so treat where foetal monitoring is available.

sources.label: Australasian Society for HIV, Viral Hepatitis and Sexual Health Medicine: Australian STI Management Guidelines
RANZCOG: Routine antenatal assessment in the absence of pregnancy complications

subtopic_detail: First line pharmacotherapy after a minimal trauma fracture in a postmenopausal woman
stem:
A 62-year-old woman attends your general practice to discuss her bone density result. Six months ago she tripped on a garden step and fractured her left distal radius, which was managed in a cast.

Her last menstrual period was at 51. She has no vasomotor symptoms now and does not want to take hormone therapy. She has never smoked, drinks two standard drinks a week, and walks 30 minutes most days. She takes no corticosteroids and has no family history of hip fracture.

Bone densitometry reports a femoral neck T-score of -2.6 and a lumbar spine T-score of -2.2. Her corrected calcium is 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D is 78 nmol/L (above 50), thyroid stimulating hormone is 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate is above 90 mL/min/1.73m2 and coeliac serology is negative. She has no reflux symptoms and can sit upright after medication.

data_table.Investigations: Femoral neck T-score -2.6, lumbar spine T-score -2.2, corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), 25-hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (above 50), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.9 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 90 mL/min/1.73m2, coeliac serology negative
data_table.History: Minimal trauma distal radius fracture 6 months ago, menopause at 51, no corticosteroid use, no reflux symptoms

options.text: Teriparatide 20 micrograms subcutaneously daily, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
options.rationale: Anabolic therapy is restricted on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme to severe established osteoporosis with a T-score of -3.0 or below plus two or more fractures, one of which must have occurred on antiresorptive therapy. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.text: Calcium 1000 mg and colecalciferol 1000 IU daily alone, with repeat densitometry in 2 years
options.rationale: Supplements support antiresorptive therapy but do not substitute for it, and her vitamin D is already adequate at 78 nmol/L; leaving a woman with a minimal trauma fracture on supplements alone forgoes proven fracture reduction. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.text: Menopausal hormone therapy with transdermal oestradiol and micronised progesterone daily
options.rationale: Hormone therapy does preserve bone density and is a reasonable choice for a woman under 60 who also wants vasomotor symptom relief, but she has no such symptoms and declines it, and it is not the first-line agent for established osteoporosis with a fracture. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
options.rationale: Denosumab is equally effective but is generally reserved for intolerance of or contraindication to oral bisphosphonates, largely because missing a dose produces rapid bone loss and a rebound risk of multiple vertebral fractures, which demands reliable 6-monthly adherence. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention

options.text: Alendronate 70 mg orally once weekly, with calcium and vitamin D intake reviewed
options.rationale: A minimal trauma fracture after the age of 50 establishes osteoporosis irrespective of the T-score and meets Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria for antiresorptive therapy, and an oral bisphosphonate is first-line because it is effective, inexpensive and forgiving of an occasional missed dose. Her normal renal function and absence of reflux make alendronate suitable. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention
Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: A minimal trauma fracture, meaning one sustained from a fall at standing height or less, defines osteoporosis clinically in anyone over 50 regardless of what the bone density shows. Secondary causes are screened for before committing to long-term therapy, which is why calcium, vitamin D, thyroid function, renal function and coeliac serology were checked here. Oral bisphosphonates are first-line in Australia, with zoledronic acid or denosumab used where oral therapy is not tolerated or absorption is doubtful. Alendronate requires an upright posture for 30 minutes with plain water on an empty stomach, so reflux, oesophageal stricture and inability to sit up are the practical contraindications. Treatment is generally reviewed after 5 years of oral therapy, when a drug holiday may be considered for lower-risk patients, whereas denosumab must never simply be stopped without transitioning to another antiresorptive.
key_points: A minimal trauma fracture after age 50 defines osteoporosis irrespective of T-score and triggers therapy
Oral bisphosphonates are first-line; denosumab and zoledronic acid follow where oral therapy is unsuitable
Screen for secondary causes with calcium, vitamin D, thyroid, renal function and coeliac serology before starting
Stopping denosumab without a follow-on antiresorptive causes rebound vertebral fractures
Anabolic therapy is reserved for severe established disease meeting strict Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme criteria
explanation.pearls: Ask about jaw pain and dental plans before starting any antiresorptive: invasive dental work is best completed beforehand, since osteonecrosis of the jaw risk on osteoporosis doses is low but concentrated around extractions.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners and Healthy Bones Australia: Osteoporosis management and fracture prevention
Australasian Menopause Society: Bone health and menopause

subtopic_detail: Uterus conserving treatment of heavy menstrual bleeding with a thickened junctional zone
stem:
A 42-year-old woman attends your gynaecology clinic with 2 years of progressively heavier periods. She now changes a super tampon hourly on her worst two days, passes clots the size of a fifty cent coin, and has taken sick leave twice this year.

Her period pain has become worse over the same period and now starts 2 days before bleeding. She has two children and does not want further pregnancies, but she is clear that she does not want a hysterectomy.

On examination the uterus is bulky, about 10 weeks in size, symmetrically enlarged and tender on bimanual palpation. Saline infusion sonohysterography shows a smooth cavity with no submucosal fibroid and an endometrial thickness of 6 mm. Magnetic resonance imaging reports a junctional zone thickness of 14 mm. An endometrial pipelle biopsy shows benign proliferative endometrium. Her haemoglobin is 98 g/L (115-155) and ferritin is 9 micrograms/L (30-200). Her cervical screening test is up to date and negative.

data_table.Examination: Symmetrically bulky tender uterus, approximately 10 weeks in size
data_table.Imaging: Saline infusion sonohysterography shows a smooth cavity with no submucosal fibroid, endometrial thickness 6 mm; magnetic resonance imaging junctional zone thickness 14 mm
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 98 g/L (115-155), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-200), endometrial pipelle biopsy benign proliferative endometrium

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation by the interventional radiology service
options.rationale: Embolisation has a role in symptomatic adenomyosis, with reported symptom improvement in many women, but it is an invasive second-line option after medical therapy has failed rather than a first recommendation. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding

options.text: Prescribe tranexamic acid 1 g three times daily for the heaviest days of each period
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid reduces menstrual loss by around a third and is a reasonable adjunct, but it does nothing for her worsening dysmenorrhoea and is less effective than the intrauterine system for bleeding of this severity. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine system at the next available appointment
options.rationale: A junctional zone of 12 mm or more on magnetic resonance imaging with a symmetrically bulky tender uterus and a normal cavity indicates adenomyosis, for which the levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the most effective uterus-conserving treatment, reducing both bleeding and dysmenorrhoea. It also provides contraception, which suits a woman who has completed her family and declines hysterectomy. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding
Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology

options.text: Refer for endometrial ablation on the next available operating theatre list
options.rationale: Ablation destroys only the superficial endometrium, so it performs poorly where glandular tissue lies deep within the myometrium, and failure rates in adenomyosis are high with a real chance of later hysterectomy. The distinguishing point against the intrauterine system is depth of disease, not severity of bleeding. (Source: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Heavy menstrual bleeding

options.text: Start a gonadotrophin releasing hormone agonist with tibolone add-back therapy
options.rationale: Agonist therapy shrinks adenomyotic tissue effectively but causes hypo-oestrogenic side effects and bone loss, so its role is short-term, usually to bridge to surgery, rather than as ongoing management at 42. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

explanation.summary: Adenomyosis is the presence of endometrial glands and stroma within the myometrium, and it is being diagnosed far more often now that magnetic resonance imaging and high-resolution transvaginal ultrasound are used to assess heavy menstrual bleeding. The classic combination is heavy bleeding with progressive dysmenorrhoea and a symmetrically bulky, tender uterus, which distinguishes it from the asymmetrical, non-tender enlargement of fibroids. A junctional zone of 12 mm or more is the accepted imaging threshold. Management in a woman who wants to keep her uterus starts with the levonorgestrel intrauterine system, with tranexamic acid, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or combined hormonal contraception as adjuncts. Iron deficiency is almost always present by the time a woman presents and should be treated in parallel, since correcting the bleeding alone will not restore her stores quickly.
key_points: A junctional zone of 12 mm or more with a symmetrically bulky tender uterus and a normal cavity indicates adenomyosis
The levonorgestrel intrauterine system is the first-line uterus-conserving treatment, helping both bleeding and pain
Endometrial ablation performs poorly in adenomyosis because the disease lies deep in the myometrium
Exclude endometrial pathology with a biopsy in women over 45, or younger with risk factors, before committing to medical therapy
Treat the accompanying iron deficiency in parallel rather than waiting for bleeding to settle
explanation.pearls: Ferritin below 30 micrograms per litre confirms iron deficiency regardless of haemoglobin, and oral iron taken on alternate days rather than daily achieves better absorption by avoiding the hepcidin rise that follows a dose.

subtopic_detail: Investigating increased liquor volume when the glucose tolerance test and antibody screen are normal
stem:
You are the registrar in a tertiary antenatal clinic. A 29-year-old woman in her second pregnancy is referred at 32 weeks because her symphysis-fundal height measures 38 cm and she feels uncomfortably stretched.

Her first pregnancy and birth were uncomplicated and that baby weighed 3.4 kg at term. She has had no fever, no rash and no contact with unwell children. She takes no medications and does not drink alcohol.

Her 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 27 weeks was normal at every time point. She is blood group O positive with a negative antibody screen. Today's ultrasound reports a single deepest vertical pocket of 9.5 cm with an amniotic fluid index of 28 cm, an estimated foetal weight on the 55th centile, normal umbilical artery Dopplers, and no hydrops. The sonographer notes that the foetal stomach was not confidently visualised on any of three attempts.

data_table.Examination: Symphysis-fundal height 38 cm at 32 weeks, tense abdomen, foetal parts difficult to palpate
data_table.Imaging: Single deepest vertical pocket 9.5 cm, amniotic fluid index 28 cm, estimated foetal weight 55th centile, normal umbilical artery Dopplers, no hydrops, foetal stomach not confidently visualised
data_table.Investigations: 75 g oral glucose tolerance test at 27 weeks normal at all time points; blood group O positive with negative antibody screen

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange a tertiary level foetal morphology ultrasound directed at swallowing and the upper gut
options.rationale: With diabetes excluded by a normal glucose tolerance test and alloimmunisation excluded by a negative antibody screen, a structural cause of impaired foetal swallowing becomes the leading explanation, and a non-visualised stomach on repeated attempts points directly to an upper gastrointestinal obstruction. Detailed imaging changes the birth plan by identifying a baby who will need a paediatric surgical centre. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test now, since gestational diabetes can develop later
options.rationale: Repeat testing is occasionally done where polyhydramnios or macrosomia appear after a normal early test, but her estimated foetal weight is on the 55th centile and the non-visualised stomach demands a structural explanation first. (Source: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines)
source_refs: Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines

options.text: Arrange maternal serology for cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis and parvovirus infection
options.rationale: Congenital infection is a recognised cause of increased liquor, but it characteristically produces hydrops, growth restriction or intracranial calcification, none of which is present, so serology is a reasonable parallel test rather than the priority. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Admit for amnioreduction to relieve her discomfort and reduce the risk of preterm labour
options.rationale: Amnioreduction is reserved for severe maternal respiratory compromise or intractable discomfort and carries risks of membrane rupture, abruption and infection; it treats a symptom without establishing the cause. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Continue two weekly growth scans with cardiotocography and review again at 36 weeks
options.rationale: Serial surveillance is appropriate once a cause has been sought and none found, but adopting it now would leave an unexplained structural finding undiagnosed until birth in a hospital that may lack paediatric surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus

explanation.summary: Polyhydramnios is defined by a single deepest vertical pocket of 8 cm or more or an amniotic fluid index above 24 cm, and about half of cases are idiopathic. The three causes that must be actively excluded are maternal diabetes, foetal structural anomalies that impair swallowing, and congenital infection or anaemia producing hydrops. Impaired swallowing covers oesophageal atresia, duodenal atresia, neurological conditions with poor swallowing and any mass effect in the neck or chest. A stomach that cannot be visualised on repeated attempts alongside increased liquor is a specific pairing that should prompt tertiary imaging and planning for delivery where paediatric surgery is available. Polyhydramnios itself increases the risk of preterm labour, malpresentation, cord prolapse at membrane rupture and postpartum haemorrhage from uterine overdistension, so the birth plan is altered even when no cause is found.
key_points: Diagnostic thresholds are a deepest vertical pocket of 8 cm or more, or an amniotic fluid index above 24 cm
Exclude maternal diabetes, foetal structural anomaly and congenital infection before accepting an idiopathic label
Increased liquor with a non-visualised foetal stomach suggests upper gastrointestinal obstruction
Anticipate malpresentation, cord prolapse at rupture of membranes and postpartum haemorrhage
Amnioreduction is symptomatic relief for severe maternal compromise, not a diagnostic step
explanation.pearls: Rupture membranes in a woman with polyhydramnios in a setting equipped for immediate caesarean, since the risk of cord prolapse is highest with a high presenting part and a sudden large fluid loss.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Prenatal assessment of the fetus
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Polyhydramnios clinical guideline
Australasian Diabetes in Pregnancy Society consensus guidelines

subtopic_detail: Timing of birth for isolated reduced liquor volume with normal growth and Dopplers
stem:
You are the registrar reviewing a 27-year-old woman in her first pregnancy at 34 weeks, referred after a growth scan arranged because of a small symphysis-fundal height measurement.

She reports normal foetal movements and denies any fluid loss, wetness or a gush at any point. She has no abdominal pain and no vaginal bleeding. Her booking blood pressure was 108/68 mmHg and it remains in that range today, with no proteinuria on dipstick.

The ultrasound reports a single deepest vertical pocket of 1.6 cm, an estimated foetal weight on the 40th centile with growth tracking along the same centile from the 28-week scan, normal umbilical artery Dopplers with positive end diastolic flow, and a normal middle cerebral artery pulsatility index. A sterile speculum examination shows no pooling and a point of care test for amniotic fluid is negative. Cardiotocography today is reactive with normal variability and no decelerations.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C, foetal heart rate 140/min
data_table.Imaging: Single deepest vertical pocket 1.6 cm, estimated foetal weight 40th centile tracking from the 28-week scan, normal umbilical artery Dopplers with positive end diastolic flow, normal middle cerebral artery pulsatility index
data_table.Investigations: Sterile speculum with no pooling, point of care amniotic fluid test negative, urine dipstick negative for protein, cardiotocography reactive with normal variability

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management plan?

options.text: Arrange delivery by caesarean section today given the reduced liquor volume around the foetus
options.rationale: Immediate delivery at 34 weeks imposes the morbidity of late preterm birth on a foetus with normal growth, normal Dopplers and a reactive cardiotocograph, none of which indicates compromise. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Timing of birth

options.text: Increase maternal oral fluid intake and repeat the liquor volume assessment in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Maternal hydration produces a small transient increase in liquor volume but does not alter outcome, and a 4-week interval leaves a pregnancy with a recognised stillbirth risk unmonitored. (Source: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline)
source_refs: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Give antenatal corticosteroids now and plan delivery in 48 hours once the course is complete
options.rationale: A corticosteroid course is appropriate when preterm birth is genuinely planned or threatened within 7 days, which is not the case here; giving it now and delivering at 34 weeks repeats the error of unnecessary late preterm birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids

options.text: Begin twice weekly foetal surveillance now with planned birth between 36 and 37 weeks
options.rationale: Isolated oligohydramnios with normal growth and normal Dopplers carries a modestly increased risk of stillbirth and intrapartum compromise without evidence of current placental insufficiency, so the balance is struck by surveillance now and birth in the late preterm to early term window rather than immediate delivery. Ruptured membranes and growth restriction have both been excluded, which is what makes this the isolated form. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Timing of birth
Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline

options.text: Continue expectant care to 40 weeks with weekly cardiotocography and no change to the plan
options.rationale: Expectant management to term ignores the observed rise in stillbirth and intrapartum compromise associated with persistently reduced liquor, and weekly monitoring alone is less than the recommended surveillance intensity. (Source: RANZCOG: Timing of birth)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Timing of birth

explanation.summary: Oligohydramnios is defined by a single deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm and the first task is always to establish whether it is isolated or a marker of another process. Ruptured membranes are excluded by history, speculum examination and a point of care test, and placental insufficiency is excluded by normal growth and normal umbilical artery Dopplers. Renal tract anomalies and exposure to non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs or angiotensin blockade are the other causes to consider. Truly isolated oligohydramnios is associated with a modest increase in stillbirth, meconium-stained liquor and cord compression in labour, which is why surveillance is intensified and birth is planned in the 36 to 37 week window rather than at term. When the liquor is low because of growth restriction, the timing decision is driven by the Doppler findings instead, and delivery is often much earlier.
key_points: A single deepest vertical pocket below 2 cm defines oligohydramnios
Exclude ruptured membranes and growth restriction before calling it isolated
Isolated oligohydramnios is managed with twice weekly surveillance and planned birth at 36 to 37 weeks
Where growth restriction coexists, Doppler findings rather than liquor volume drive the timing of birth
Ask about non-steroidal anti-inflammatory and renin-angiotensin drug exposure, and check the foetal renal tract
explanation.pearls: The single deepest vertical pocket is preferred over the amniotic fluid index for diagnosing oligohydramnios, because the index diagnoses more cases and leads to more inductions and caesareans without improving perinatal outcome.

sources.label: Royal Women's Hospital Victoria: Oligohydramnios clinical guideline
